title: Restraining orders in family cases
intro: This guide describes, in general terms, the restraining orders available under section 46 of Ontario's Family Law Act and section 35 of the Children's Law Reform Act: who may apply, against whom, and what an order may contain. It explains what the law says; it does not say whether an order is available in any particular situation.

sections.heading: Two laws that provide restraining orders
paragraphs: Two Ontario laws let a family court make a restraining order: section 46 of the Family Law Act and section 35 of the Children's Law Reform Act. Under both, the court may make “an interim or final restraining order”. (Family Law Act, s. 46 (1); Children's Law Reform Act, s. 35 (1))

In the Family Law Act, “court” means “the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice or the Superior Court of Justice”. In Part III of the Children's Law Reform Act, where section 35 appears, “court” means “the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court or the Superior Court of Justice”. (Family Law Act, s. 1 (1); Children's Law Reform Act, s. 18 (1))

sections.heading: Who can apply under the Family Law Act
paragraphs: The wording of section 46 now in force says: “On application, the court may make an interim or final restraining order against a person described in subsection (2) if the applicant has reasonable grounds to fear for his or her own safety or for the safety of any child in his or her lawful custody.” (Family Law Act, s. 46 (1))

Under the wording now in force, the order may be made against “a spouse or former spouse of the applicant”, or against a person other than a spouse or former spouse of the applicant, “if the person is cohabiting with the applicant or has cohabited with the applicant for any period of time.” (Family Law Act, s. 46 (2))
The Act defines “cohabit” as “to live together in a conjugal relationship, whether within or outside marriage”. (Family Law Act, s. 1 (1))

Section 46 is in Part III of the Act, where “spouse” means a spouse as defined in subsection 1 (1) and also includes either of two persons who are not married to each other and have cohabited “continuously for a period of not less than three years”, or “in a relationship of some permanence, if they are the parents of a child as set out in section 4 of the Children’s Law Reform Act.” (Family Law Act, s. 29)

sections.heading: Who can apply under the Children's Law Reform Act
paragraphs: The wording of section 35 now in force says: “On application, the court may make an interim or final restraining order against any person if the applicant has reasonable grounds to fear for his or her own safety or for the safety of any child in his or her lawful custody.” (Children's Law Reform Act, s. 35 (1))
Unlike section 46 of the Family Law Act, section 35 does not limit who the order may be made against: it says “against any person”. (Children's Law Reform Act, s. 35 (1); Family Law Act, s. 46 (2))

sections.heading: What an order can include
paragraphs: Under both laws, a restraining order “shall be in the form prescribed by the rules of court and may contain one or more of the following provisions, as the court considers appropriate”. (Family Law Act, s. 46 (3); Children's Law Reform Act, s. 35 (2))

The provisions listed in the wording now in force are: “Restraining the respondent, in whole or in part, from directly or indirectly contacting or communicating with the applicant or any child in the applicant’s lawful custody.”; “Restraining the respondent from coming within a specified distance of one or more locations.”; “Specifying one or more exceptions to the provisions described in paragraphs 1 and 2.”; and “Any other provision that the court considers appropriate.” (Family Law Act, s. 46 (3); Children's Law Reform Act, s. 35 (2))

sections.heading: Forms and court procedure
paragraphs: Under the Family Law Rules, a restraining order under section 35 of the Children's Law Reform Act or section 46 of the Family Law Act “shall be in Form 25F or 25G.” The rules' table of forms lists Form 25F as “RESTRAINING ORDER” and Form 25G as “RESTRAINING ORDER ON MOTION WITHOUT NOTICE”. (Family Law Rules, r. 25 (11.1); Table of Forms)

An order terminating one of these restraining orders “shall be in Form 25H.” The clerk prepares a restraining order, or an order terminating one, for signature “as soon as it is made”. (Family Law Rules, r. 25 (11) (b), (11.2))

The mandatory information program in rule 8.1 applies to cases started after August 31, 2011 that deal with, among other things, “A restraining order under the Family Law Act or the Children’s Law Reform Act.” Each party attends “no later than 45 days after the case is started”, subject to the exceptions in subrule 8.1 (2). (Family Law Rules, r. 8.1 (1), (2), (4))

On motion, the court may order that any or all of the program's attendance requirements in subrules 8.1 (4) to (7) do not apply to a party “because of urgency or hardship or for some other reason in the interest of justice.” (Family Law Rules, r. 8.1 (8))

“In a proceeding for corollary relief” under the Divorce Act, the court has a duty to consider whether “a civil protection order or a proceeding in relation to such an order” is pending or in effect, unless it “would clearly not be appropriate to do so”. (Divorce Act, s. 7.8 (2))

sections.heading: Amendments that are not yet in force
paragraphs: The published text of both sections also prints replacement wording passed in 2025. For section 46, the Act notes that “On a day to be named by order of the Lieutenant Governor in Council, subsection 46 (1) of the Act is repealed and the following substituted”. Its amendment table lists “2025, c. 6, Sched. 6, s. 1 (1, 2) - not in force”. This guide describes only the wording now in force. (Family Law Act, s. 46)
Section 35 of the Children's Law Reform Act carries the same kind of note, and its amendment table lists “2025, c. 6, Sched. 2, s. 1 (1-3) - not in force”. (Children's Law Reform Act, s. 35)

Each section also says that the section “as it read on October 14, 2009, continues to apply to” proceedings begun under it before October 15, 2009 and to orders made under it that were in force on October 14, 2009. (Family Law Act, s. 46 (4); Children's Law Reform Act, s. 35 (3))

sections.heading: If an order is not followed
paragraphs: The Family Law Act gives the Ontario Court of Justice a power, “In addition to its powers in respect of contempt”, to punish by fine or imprisonment, or by both, “any wilful contempt of or resistance to its process, rules or orders under this Act, other than orders under section 46”. The Children's Law Reform Act has a similar provision that excludes “orders under section 35”. (Family Law Act, s. 49 (1); Children's Law Reform Act, s. 38 (1))

Neither section 46 of the Family Law Act nor section 35 of the Children's Law Reform Act sets out what happens if a restraining order is breached. This site does not yet have a source on the consequences of breaching a restraining order. (Family Law Act, ss. 46, 49 (1); Children's Law Reform Act, ss. 35, 38 (1))
